title: Cheeks
description: Conditions affecting the buccal mucosa, from benign keratotic variants to inflammatory and potentially malignant lesions.

problems.description: Recurrent shallow ulcers on the inner cheek, appearing in crops and healing without scarring within a fortnight.
problems.etiology:
An immunologically mediated reaction in genetically susceptible individuals: a T-cell attack on the non-keratinized mucosa [1]. The reason the buccal mucosa is so commonly affected is that it's exactly the kind of non-keratinized surface where RAS favours developing [2].

Several triggers can kick off or worsen attacks:

- **Haematinic deficiency**: iron, vitamin B12, or folate deficiency can precipitate or worsen episodes [1, 3].
- **Systemic disease**: gastrointestinal conditions — Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, coeliac disease — are recognised associations [1].
- **Local trauma**: mucosal injury (sharp restoration edge, anaesthetised biting) can localise an ulcer to that site [4].
- **Medications**: nicorandil, NSAIDs, alendronic acid, methotrexate [1, 3].
- **Hormonal / stress**: fall in progesterone at menstruation, stress [1].
- **Smoking cessation**: paradoxically, stopping smoking can precipitate ulceration [3].
problems.presentation:
The patient reports painful mouth ulcers that come and go, usually starting in childhood or adolescence, and settle completely between episodes. What you see on examination:

- **Shallow ulcers**, 2–5 mm diameter, with a well-defined margin and erythematous halo [2, 5].
- **Buccal mucosa** is the site shown in the classic presentation — anterior buccal mucosa and labial mucosa are the typical locations [5].
- Usually 1–6 ulcers at a time; heal within 1–2 weeks without leaving a scar [1].
- Prodromal burning discomfort may precede the ulcer by a day [1].
problems.results:
Diagnosis is clinical. Investigations are for **underlying causes**, not the ulcers themselves:

- **FBC and haematinics** (iron, ferritin, B12, folate): look for haematinic deficiency, which can worsen or precipitate RAS [1, 3].
- **Serum antiendomysium and transglutaminase assay**: to exclude coeliac disease [1].
- **No scarring on examination**: distinguishes minor from major RAS [5].
- **No systemic illness, no fever**: distinguishes from primary herpetic stomatitis, which presents with constitutional upset.
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The thing that separates RAS from its near-neighbours:

- **Unlike traumatic ulcers**: RAS is recurrent and episodic — there's a clear history of ulcers coming and going over years [5]. A traumatic ulcer is single and resolves once the cause is removed.
- **Unlike herpetiform ulcers**: minor RAS ulcers are 2–5 mm, appear in small crops, and don't coalesce. Herpetiform RAS mimics herpetic stomatitis — up to 100 tiny ulcers, often on the floor of mouth and tongue margins [1].
- **Unlike major RAS**: minor RAS heals within 2 weeks and leaves no scar. Major RAS ulcers exceed 10 mm, last 5–10 weeks, and scar on healing [1].
- **Unlike erythema multiforme**: RAS has no 'target' skin lesions, no fever, and is confined to the non-keratinized mucosa. EM causes more widespread, irregular bullous erosions [5].

A recent change in frequency or severity always triggers a search for an underlying systemic cause [3].
problems.treatment:
The goal is to reduce duration and frequency — no treatment cures the condition [6].

**First line:**

- **Chlorhexidine mouthwash** (0.2%) to prevent secondary infection and reduce severity [1].
- **Benzydamine hydrochloride mouthwash** for analgesia during an attack [6].
- **Hydrocortisone pellets** (2.5 mg) dissolved in contact with the ulcer — topical steroid [6].
- **Topical tetracycline** and steroid preparations are sometimes useful [1].

**Identify and treat any underlying cause:** haematinic replacement under GP, dietary review for coeliac, medication review [1, 3].

**Advise patient to switch** to a sodium lauryl sulfate-free toothpaste if SLS is a trigger [1].
problems.prognosis: Minor RAS is a nuisance rather than a harmful condition [6]. With identification and treatment of any underlying deficiency, the pattern typically settles back to the baseline — occasional single ulcers. Without addressing an underlying cause, the worsening pattern persists. The condition often remits spontaneously over years, but some patients have attacks continuously into adulthood.

citations.quote: Recurrent aphthous stomatitis (RAS) is the term given to a fairly well-defined group of conditions characterized by recurrent oral ulceration. There are three subgroups: A very common condition (~25% of population) affecting ~80% of RAS patients. Start at childhood or adolescence. Usually appear as a group of 1–6 ulcers at a time, of variable size (usually 2–5mm diameter). Mainly occur on non-keratinized mucosa and heal within 1–2 weeks without scarring. Usually recur at an interval of 1–4 months. Prodromal discomfort may precede painful ulcers. Exacerbated by stress, local trauma, menstruation (fall in progesterone level), sodium lauryl sulfate (in some toothpastes), drugs (NSAIDs, alendronic acid, and nicorandil), smoking, allergy to some foods, and may be an oral 'marker' of iron, vitamin B12, or folate deficiencies. In some cases, they are a manifestation of Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, or gluten enteropathy. Aetiology, although not fully understood, is almost certainly a T-cell-mediated immunological reaction in patients with a genetic predisposition (HLA A1, A11, B12, and DR2). There is a familial history in 45% of cases. Rx: prevent superinfection with chlorhexidine mouthwash and relieve pain (simple analgesics, benzydamine mouthrinse). Topical tetracycline and steroid preparations are sometimes useful. It is important to look for and treat any underlying deficiency or coexisting pathology (FBC, haematinics, vitamin B12 and red cell folate, serum antiendomysium, and transglutaminase assay).
Classically, aphthous ulceration affects the non-keratinized mucosa although it is not an exclusive finding.

Medications must be considered as a potential cause for oral ulceration. Review the medication history to ensure that nothing has been missed. Check for medication side effects in the British National Formulary (BNF) and assess whether the ulcer history coincides with recent prescription of a new medication, or a change in the dose of an existing medication. Medication causes of oral ulceration include nicorandil, used for management of angina, and methotrexate, which is used for such conditions as rheumatoid arthritis. Smoking cessation should be excluded by questioning. Ulceration related to smoking cessation can be difficult to manage, often not responding well to topical therapies.

Remember that aphthae often develop at the sites of minor trauma. Mucosal trauma during restoration placement, from a sharp edge on the restoration, or from biting while the mucosa was anaesthetized might well explain the location of this particular ulcer.

There is an obvious ulcer on the anterior buccal mucosa. It is shallow, a few millimetres in diameter and has a slightly irregular but well-defined margin. There is a halo of erythema around the ulcer, but the surrounding mucosa is otherwise unremarkable. The appearance alone is not particularly helpful in differential diagnosis but is typical of minor recurrent aphthous stomatitis. If you were able to examine the patient, you would find no evidence of scarring, supporting the diagnosis of recurrent aphthous stomatitis minor, as opposed to recurrent aphthous stomatitis major.

RAS is very common and is a 'nuisance' condition rather than one that is harmful to health. Although many treatments are available, none will 'cure' the ulcers. Rather, the goal of treatment is to reduce the duration and frequency of oral ulceration. In the meantime, a mouthwash such as benzydamine hydrochloride may improve the patient's comfort. Prescription of hydrocortisone pellets could also be considered.

problems.description: Bilateral lacy white lines on the inner cheeks in a middle-aged woman; no ulceration, no pain.
problems.etiology:
A chronic autoimmune inflammatory disease in which T-lymphocytes attack stratified squamous epithelia [1]. The result is hyperkeratosis of the epithelium and a characteristic histological pattern of hyperparakeratosis, elongated saw-tooth rete ridges, and a dense sub-epithelial lymphocyte band.

The usual trigger is unknown, but two exogenous patterns exist:

- **Lichenoid reactions to systemic drugs**: gold (classically), NSAIDs, oral hypoglycaemics, beta blockers, ACE inhibitors [2, 3].
- **Lichenoid reactions to dental materials**: amalgam restorations in direct contact with, or close to, the lesion [4].

The oral lesions persist longer than skin lesions. Females are affected more commonly than males at 3:2. The condition affects up to 2% of the general population [1].
problems.presentation:
Patients are often asymptomatic and the lesion is noticed incidentally. What they describe when symptomatic: a rough, slightly sore feeling in the cheeks, not sharp pain.

What you see:

- **Bilateral reticular white striae** on the posterior buccal mucosa — the classic Wickham's striae pattern [1].
- Not present on the palate; can affect tongue, lips, and gingivae [1].
- **Bilateral symmetry** is characteristic — unilateral disease should make you think lichenoid reaction rather than lichen planus [5].
- Associated with brown pigmentation at the periphery of striae in some patients, from melanin drop-out [6].
- Skin involvement in some cases: purple itchy papules on the flexor surfaces of the wrists and shins [1].
problems.results:
- **Biopsy**: confirms the diagnosis when presentation is atypical or when dysplasia needs to be excluded. Histology shows dense band-like lymphocytic infiltrate, basal cell degeneration, and saw-tooth rete ridges [6].
- **Candidal smear or saliva culture**: thick keratotic epithelium is prone to superimposed candidal infection, which worsens symptoms [7].
- **Autoantibody screen (ANA, ENA, dsDNA)**: indicated if lupus erythematosus is a possibility — typically negative in lichen planus [8].
- **Medication review**: identify potential lichenoid drug offenders; check whether distribution of lesions corresponds to any restoration [5].
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The key distinguishing features:

- **Bilateral and posterior buccal mucosa**: this is nearly pathognomonic for lichen planus. A lichenoid reaction tends to be unilateral, more acute in onset, often with extensive ulceration and asymmetrical distribution [5].
- **Wickham's striae vs plaque**: reticular lichen planus has the characteristic lacy net pattern. Plaque-type lichen planus forms white patches without the striae, and is more common in smokers — this presentation is harder to distinguish from leukoplakia [9].
- **Not palatal**: oral lichen planus does not typically affect the hard palate — lesions there should prompt thinking about lupus erythematosus [8].
- **Unlike erosive lichen planus**: reticular lichen planus has no ulceration or erythematous areas. The reticular type carries no proven premalignant potential [10]. The erosive variant is the one that requires 6-monthly malignancy surveillance.
problems.treatment:
Asymptomatic reticular lichen planus needs **reassurance only** — no active treatment required [2].

When symptomatic (sore, burning, ulceration):

- **Topical steroids**: betamethasone 0.5 mg dissolved in 5–10 mL water as a mouthwash, rinsed for 2–3 minutes up to three times daily [11].
- Alternatively: prednisolone mouthwash or topical dexamethasone [2].
- For stubborn or widespread disease, oral steroids, azathioprine, topical tacrolimus, or tretinoin gel in tertiary care [2].
- **Plaque control**: gingival involvement is worsened by plaque; help the patient maintain optimal oral hygiene [7].
- **SLS-free toothpaste**: sodium lauryl sulfate can irritate the lesions [7].
- **Identify and remove drug triggers** if lichenoid reaction is suspected [2].

Erosive lichen planus (with red, ulcerated areas) warrants specialist referral and 6-monthly follow-up.
problems.prognosis: Reticular lichen planus has **no proven premalignant potential** [10]. It can last for months or years — lesions persist longer in the mouth than on skin. Symptomatic control is achievable with topical steroids. Malignant transformation risk is very low overall, estimated at less than 0.1% [12], and concentrated in the erosive rather than the reticular variant.

citations.quote: This is a chronic inflammatory disease of adults involving skin and mucous membranes. It affects up to 2% of the general population; 50% of patients with skin lesions have oral lesions, whereas 25% have oral lesions alone. The oral lesions persist longer than the skin lesions. It affects females more commonly than males at the ratio of 3:2. It is an autoimmune condition mediated by a T-lymphocyte attack on stratified squamous epithelia which leads to hyperkeratosis and the typical histological appearance. Usually the oral lesions are bilateral and posterior in the buccal mucosa; it is not seen on the palate but can, however, affect the tongue, lips, gingivae, and floor of mouth. The most common oral lesion is a lacy reticular pattern of hyperkeratotic epithelia seen bilaterally on the buccal mucosa.

Rx: biopsy may be indicated to exclude dysplasia or malignancy; if there are lichenoid eruptions, the implicated drugs should be identified and avoided if possible. Reassurance for asymptomatic reticular lesions. If painful or if ulceration is present, topical steroids such as betamethasone (at least 1mg rinsed for 3min tds–qds), prednisolone mouthwash or topical dexamethasone are usually helpful. In severe cases, oral steroids, azathioprine, topical tacrolimus, or tretinoin gel may be used in 3° care setting. Erosive type lichen planus should be followed up 6-monthly to exclude the transformation to malignancy.
Classically associated with the use of gold in the Rx of rheumatoid arthritis. NSAIDs, oral hypoglycaemics, and beta blockers are commoner offenders.
In addition, there is a link between allergy to constituents of dental amalgam and lichenoid eruptions in the oral cavity in certain individuals.

Some features that point to a lichenoid drug reaction rather than lichen planus include acute onset, extensive ulceration, asymmetrical distribution and severe involvement of the dorsum of the tongue. Lesions may also affect sites that are less commonly affected by lichen planus such as the floor of the mouth. Lichenoid reactions may be clinically indistinguishable from lichen planus.

The dense band-like infiltrate of lymphocytes and lymphocytic infiltration of the basal cells with focal basal cell degeneration, apoptosis, loss of basal cells and a thickened basement membrane are typical of lichen planus.

Gingival lichen planus is aggravated by plaque, and in some patients, maintaining optimal oral hygiene can be difficult because of pain. Patients should be helped to maintain a high standard of oral hygiene. Some patients also find the detergent sodium lauryl sulphate (SLS) in certain toothpastes an irritant, and they should switch to an SLS-free toothpaste. When lichen planus or a lichenoid reaction is widespread or becomes symptomatic, the possibility of superimposed candidal infection should be considered. The thick keratotic epithelium is more prone to infection compared with normal epithelium.

Lesions in LE often have a central ulcer or erythematous area around which the striae tend to radiate, rather than follow the random pattern of lichen planus. Lesions are also typically asymmetrical and affect the hard and soft palates, which are less frequently involved by lichen planus or lichenoid reactions.

Lichen planus and lichenoid reactions may cause homogeneous white patches. This more unusual presentation seems to be more common in smokers, and it is not at all clear whether these so-called plaque-type lichen planus lesions are a genuine presentation of lichen planus or are induced by smoking.
The typical appearance of reticular pattern oral lichen planus, a condition with no premalignant potential (this is found in the erosive variant).
In this case, the oral symptoms were managed with 0.5 mg betamethasone dissolved in 5–10 ml water as a mouthwash for 2–3 minutes up to three times daily.

There is also a very low risk of malignant transformation in oral lichen planus. There is controversy surrounding the exact rate of malignant transformation, but it is likely to be less than 0.1%. Some authorities suggest that malignant change is more common in nonreticular forms of oral lichen planus.

problems.description: A rough white patch on the inner cheek lining that developed gradually and won't rub off; no clear cause found.
problems.etiology:
Leukoplakia is a diagnosis of exclusion: a white patch that cannot be characterised as any other lesion after all known causes have been eliminated [1]. The largest single group has no identifiable cause.

Where a cause is identifiable, tobacco is the leading culprit:

- Smoking (low-grade burn plus chemical irritants) and alcohol act **synergistically** as the main aetiological factors [2].
- Buccal leukoplakia at the site of paan quid placement carries a high risk of malignant change if the habit continues [3].
- Idiopathic (non-smoking) leukoplakia is actually **more likely to transform** than smoker's leukoplakia [4].

The histopathology ranges widely from essentially benign keratosis to carcinoma in situ — the degree of dysplasia is the key variable [3].
problems.presentation:
Often asymptomatic; found incidentally at a dental check-up. The patient may describe a rough patch.

What you see:

- A **white, non-removable plaque** on the buccal mucosa; the postcommissural region is a classic site [5].
- Flat and homogeneous in low-risk lesions. **Red or speckled areas** (erythroleukoplakia) raise the concern for dysplasia or early carcinoma [6].
- Lesion is more **sharply defined** than frictional keratosis, which typically blends gradually into adjacent mucosa [5].
problems.results:
- **Biopsy is required** as a general rule for all non-removable white patches [7]. Even clinically innocuous-looking lesions occasionally conceal carcinoma.
- Histopathology assesses: degree of dysplasia (mild, moderate, severe), presence of Candida hyphae in the superficial keratin [8].
- Overall malignant transformation rate is **12.1%** across all leukoplakias; significant difference between mild/moderate and severe dysplasia (10.3% vs 24.1%) [4].
- At floor of mouth or ventral tongue, >25% may progress [3].
- **Toluidine blue** staining can guide biopsy site selection but has limited predictive value — false positives are common [9].
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The distinction that matters most is from conditions that look similar but have a known cause:

- **Frictional keratosis**: found along the occlusal line; associated with a sharp tooth or restoration; merges gradually into normal mucosa; resolves on removing the cause [5].
- **Chronic hyperplastic candidosis**: arises on the postcommissural buccal mucosa; associated with red areas; resolves after systemic antifungals — biopsy and resolution with treatment are the most reliable distinguishing tests [5].
- **Lichen planus plaque type**: look for more typical bilateral reticular striae elsewhere in the mouth or on the skin [5].
- **Squamous cell carcinoma**: must be included for any white patch without an identified cause — especially if speckled, indurated, ulcerated, or in a high-risk site [6].

Idiopathic white patch is what remains after all these are excluded.
problems.treatment:
**All patients with leukoplakia should stop smoking and moderate alcohol** [10].

Management depends on degree of dysplasia:

- **Mild or no dysplasia**: monitor closely — 3-monthly initially, then 6-monthly, then annual review. Repeat biopsy if change is noted [10].
- **Moderate or severe dysplasia**: laser or knife excision. If too large for excision, close monitoring to detect transformation [10].
- **Candidal infection**: treat with systemic antifungals (fluconazole or itraconazole); correct associated iron, folate, and B12 deficiency; patients should stop smoking [8].
- **Referral**: any suspicion of malignancy — red or speckled areas, induration, ulceration, palpable nodes — warrants urgent specialist referral [7].
problems.prognosis: Overall transformation rate is 12.1% [4]. Malignant transformation is more common in idiopathic (non-smoker) leukoplakia than in smoker's leukoplakia [4]. Risk is highest in lesions with severe dysplasia (24.1%) and at high-risk sites (floor of mouth, ventral tongue). Dysplasia does not always progress — mild dysplasia may regress in some cases [11]. With cessation of tobacco and alcohol and close follow-up, the minority of lesions that do transform are ideally caught early.

citations.quote: The literal meaning of leukoplakia is 'white patch'. The term is correctly defined as a white patch that cannot be characterized as any other lesion. The use of this term is correct only after all possible known causes have been eliminated through whatever investigations are required.
Excessive alcohol and tobacco use are the important factors in the aetiology of cancer of the mouth showing a 'synergistic effect'.

The histopathology of these lesions varies widely from the essentially benign to carcinoma in situ. The degree of dysplasia is one of the most important factors to be considered in the management of a leucoplakia. Third, relation to cause, e.g. buccal leucoplakia, the preferred site for a paan quid is at high risk of malignant change if the habit is not discontinued.

One meta-analysis revealed that the overall malignant transformation rate of leucoplakia was 12.1% and there was a significant difference between mild/moderate and severe dysplasia (10.3% vs 24.1%). Malignant transformation is more common among non-smokers (idiopathic leucoplakia).

Frictional keratosis is common along the occlusal line, on edentulous alveolar ridges and on the lateral tongue. It may be associated with sharp teeth or restoration(s) and be unilateral or bilateral. Frictional keratosis usually merges gradually with the surrounding normal mucosa and is not as sharply defined as the present lesion. Chronic hyperplastic candidosis (candidal 'leukoplakia') forms a discrete white plaque that is sometimes associated with red areas. Unless the site is typical, it is almost impossible to make the diagnosis clinically. Biopsy and resolution following antifungal treatment are the most useful indications to identify these lesions.

Squamous cell carcinoma diagnosis must be included for any white patch in the mouth without an identified cause. Although it is in a high-risk site, it is a flat, homogeneous lesion without ulceration, red areas, speckling or induration. The patient is a light smoker and is in the risk age group for squamous cell carcinoma.

Yes. As a general rule, all white lesions in the mouth require biopsy. Completely typical keratotic lichen planus and typical frictional keratoses are considered exceptions to this rule by some authorities, but this would only be acceptable if the clinician were very experienced in the diagnosis of oral white lesions. If there is any suspicion of malignancy, the patient should be referred to a specialist centre via an expedited referral pathway, according to local and national protocols.

This is more commonly seen in middle-aged men who are heavy smokers. It typically presents as a white patch on the oral commissural buccal mucosa bilaterally or dorsum of tongue. Although there is an ↑ risk of malignant change, the initial approach after ensuring the diagnosis microbiologically and histopathologically is to eradicate the candidal infection. Rx: systemic antifungals such as fluconazole and itraconazole are indicated. Often associated with iron, folate, and vitamin B12 deficiency, and smoking, which should be corrected. Most lesions will resolve after such Rx; if not, reassess degree of dysplasia and surgical excision may be indicated.

Toluidine blue (tolonium chloride) staining was described decades ago but its use has recently been revived in the form of new commercial test kits. The predictive value of the test remains unclear, with better results shown in high-risk populations. False-positive reactions are common because the dye binds to ulcer slough, staining ulcers, lichen planus and other benign lesions.

The patient should stop smoking and moderate her alcohol intake. In this case, and others in which dysplasia is mild or absent, it is appropriate to monitor the lesion closely for changes in appearance, initially at 3-monthly intervals and then extending to annual review, provided the lesion does not change significantly. Lesions with moderate or severe dysplasia may be removed through knife or laser excision.

Dysplasia does not always progress, and in some cases of mild dysplasia, it may regress. Dysplasia indicates increased potential for malignant transformation but does not necessarily mean that this may eventually occur in any particular lesion.

problems.description: A white cheek patch that resolves when the source of repeated friction is removed.
problems.etiology:
A white patch caused by **hyperplastic hyperkeratotic epithelium** induced by repeated local trauma [1]. The epithelium thickens in response to chronic friction — essentially a protective keratinisation. Common sources:

- Cheek biting (morsicatio buccarum) — habitual or parafunctional
- A sharp tooth edge or fractured cusp
- An ill-fitting denture flange
- A rough or overhanging restoration margin [1]

In psychiatric disorders or learning disability, cheek biting can be a form of self-mutilation [1].
problems.presentation:
Often asymptomatic; the patient may notice a rough area on the inside of their cheek, or the dentist spots it on routine examination.

What you see:

- **White patch** on the buccal mucosa, usually at the **occlusal plane** — the line where the teeth meet [2].
- The lesion **merges gradually** into the surrounding normal mucosa — less sharply defined than leukoplakia [2].
- In cheek biters: the surface is often **shredded or ragged**, with similar lesions on both sides of the commissure [2].
- Clear association with an adjacent sharp tooth, denture flange, or restoration identifiable on examination.
problems.results:
Diagnosis is clinical, confirmed by resolution:

- **Remove the cause** (smooth sharp tooth, rebase denture, polish restoration) and observe: frictional keratosis resolves completely [1].
- **If it doesn't resolve after removing the cause**: biopsy is indicated to exclude dysplasia or carcinoma [1].
- No special tests required in the first instance.
problems.definingCharacteristics:
Frictional keratosis differs from leukoplakia in two key ways: there is a **clear identifiable cause** (friction) and the lesion **resolves when the cause is removed** [1]. If the white patch persists after eliminating the friction source, the frictional keratosis diagnosis fails and biopsy is mandatory.

Distinguishing from candidal leukoplakia: frictional keratosis occurs at the occlusal line; candidal leukoplakia typically forms on the postcommissural buccal mucosa and is associated with red areas [2]. Unlike lichen planus, frictional keratosis has no bilateral symmetry and no striae pattern — it tracks the mechanical insult.
problems.treatment:
**Remove the friction source** — the whole treatment in uncomplicated cases [1]:

- Smooth any sharp tooth edge or cusp.
- Replace or rebase an ill-fitting denture.
- Polish or replace the offending restoration.
- Address cheek-biting habit — habit awareness, occlusal splint if needed.

If resolution is incomplete after a reasonable interval, **biopsy to exclude dysplasia** [1].
problems.prognosis: Excellent with cause removal: complete resolution is the expected outcome [1]. No premalignant potential in true frictional keratosis. The risk is in misclassifying a leukoplakia or early carcinoma as frictional keratosis — the resolution test is the critical safety check.

citations.quote: This is a white patch due to hyperplastic hyperkeratotic epithelium induced by local trauma, e.g. sharp tooth, denture, or cheek biting. It is managed by removal of the source of the friction, which will generally allow complete resolution of the lesion. If this doesn't happen, biopsy is indicated. Can be seen as self-mutilation in psychiatric disorders or learning disability.

Frictional keratosis is common along the occlusal line, on edentulous alveolar ridges and on the lateral tongue. It may be associated with sharp teeth or restoration(s) and be unilateral or bilateral. Frictional keratosis usually merges gradually with the surrounding normal mucosa and is not as sharply defined as the present lesion. Tongue biting also causes keratosis, but the surface is often shredded, and there may be similar lesions on the buccal mucosa, usually just behind the commissure.

problems.description: A non-healing, firm, indurated ulcer or mixed red-white patch on the cheek in a smoker or heavy drinker.
problems.etiology:
Over 90% of oral cancers are SCCs [1]. Buccal SCC is not the most common oral site (floor of mouth accounts for >75% of European and American cases [2]), but the buccal mucosa is a high-risk site when paan/betel quid is the driver.

Main aetiological factors:

- **Tobacco and alcohol**: act synergistically as the primary risk factors for buccal and all oral SCC. Combined relative risk is at least 5–10 times higher than a non-smoker/occasional drinker [3].
- **Betel quid / paan chewing**: the most clear-cut single aetiological factor; the buccal sulcus where the quid sits is directly at risk [1].
- **HPV 16 and 18**: an independent risk factor, primarily for oropharyngeal SCC [1].
- **Immunosuppression** (renal transplant, HIV): increases risk [1].

Pain is a late feature — early buccal SCC is often painless [4].
problems.presentation:
The patient may present with a lump, a non-healing sore, or come in for another reason and have the lesion found incidentally.

What you see:

- **Painless indurated ulcer** with raised, rolled edges, granular base, fixed to surrounding tissues [4].
- Alternatively: a **speckled (mixed red and white) patch** — erythroleukoplakia — on the buccal mucosa [4].
- **Induration on palpation**: firmer than adjacent mucosa [5].
- **Cervical lymphadenopathy**: may be the first presentation if nodal spread has occurred [4].
- Malignancy should be suspected if any suspicious lesion persists **>3 weeks** [4].
problems.results:
- **Biopsy is mandatory**: urgent referral to a specialist centre for same-day or expedited referral if malignancy is suspected [6].
- **Histology**: shows invasion of deep tissues, cellular pleomorphism, increased nuclear staining [7].
- **CT/MRI and FNAC of neck nodes** to stage the disease and assess for cervical lymph node involvement [8].
- **Staging**: prognosis for stage I is >85% 5-year survival; for stage IV is 10% [9].
- Nodal involvement reduces cure rates by 50% [9].
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The features that should stop you in your tracks:

- **Induration** — firmness on palpation is a cardinal sign of malignancy. Leukoplakia, lichen planus, and frictional keratosis are not indurated [5].
- **Persistence >3 weeks**: a benign traumatic ulcer heals within 2 weeks on removing the cause. An SCC does not [4].
- **Speckled appearance or erythroplakia component**: most of these lesions are carcinoma in situ or frank carcinoma [10].
- **Fixed to underlying tissues**: inflammatory ulcers and RAS are not fixed.

The combination of tobacco + alcohol + the right age group (sixth and seventh decades, though incidence is rising in younger patients [2]) + a non-healing lesion in a buccal site used for paan: refer same day.
problems.treatment:
Not primarily managed in general dental practice:

- **Urgent/same-day referral** to a specialist centre when malignancy is suspected — do not biopsy in the practice if the plan is to refer [6].
- Specialist treatment: surgery, followed by radiotherapy with or without chemotherapy, depending on stage and histological features of the excised tumour [11].
- Patients should be encouraged to stop smoking — smoking-associated cardiovascular disease can compromise treatment [11].
- Neck dissection may be required even when no lymph node metastasis is detectable (approximately 25% of deposits are occult metastases not visible on imaging) [12].
problems.prognosis: Stage-dependent. Stage I: >85% 5-year survival. Stage IV: 10% at 5 years [9]. Nodal involvement halves cure rates [9]. Overall oral cancer mortality rate is just over 50% despite treatment [1]. If treated early, a 5-year survival of 85% or better can be achieved, and survival to 10 years is considered cure [11]. Approximately 10% of patients develop a second primary in the mouth or upper aerodigestive tract [11].

citations.quote: Cancer of the mouth accounts for ~2% of all malignant tumours in northern Europe and the US, but ~30–40% in the Indian subcontinent. >90% of these are SCCs. Globally it is the sixth commonest cause of cancer-related death. >2000 new cases of oral cancer are registered per year in the UK and each year half that number die from or with the disease. Overall mortality rate is just over 50% despite Rx.

The floor of the mouth is the commonest single site, accounting for >75% of carcinomas seen in European or American practice. The other high-risk sites are the retromolar region and lateral tongue. Most common in sixth and seventh decades, however there appears to be an increasing incidence in younger patients and those who do not use tobacco.

She drinks 14 units of alcohol per week, which is the maximum recommended intake. The maximum intake is considered 'safe' in terms of liver and cardiovascular disease risks, but no safe limit is recognized for cancer. There is no safe intake for tobacco, and the combined relative risk of carcinoma for this patient is at least 5–10 times higher than that for a nonsmoker or an occasional drinker.

Oral cancer is most often seen as a painless ulcer, although it may present as a swelling or as an area of leucoplakia, erythroleucoplakia, or erythroplakia. Malignancy should be suspected if any of these lesions persists for >3 weeks. Pain is usually a late feature. The ulcer is described as firm with raised edges, with an indurated, inflamed, granular base and is fixed to surrounding tissues.
Palpation reveals the lesion to be firmer than the adjacent mucosa. The white component of the area cannot be rubbed away.

No, definitely not. Although removing a sample of the tissue is well within the capability of the general dental practitioner, it would be unwise to do so. The patient will return for the result, and dental practitioners are not usually the appropriate persons to break the news of malignant disease to the patient. In a practice environment, the patient should be referred urgently, preferably the same day, to a centre where definitive treatment can be provided.

Mostly SCC. Characteristically shows invasion of deep tissues with cellular pleomorphism and ↑ nuclear staining. The presence of a lymphocytic response may have prognostic value, as does the manner of invasion (pushing or spreading). Can spread via local infiltration or lymphatic system (cervical nodes), and late spread via bloodstream.

After the biopsy, further investigations including computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) showed no cervical lymph node metastasis in this patient.

This is dependent on site and stage, (prognosis for stage I is >85% and for stage IV is 10% over 5yrs), and co-morbidity. The presence or absence of extracapsular spread of tumour in metastatic cervical nodes is the most important single prognostic factor. Nodal involvement ↓ cure rates by 50%.

This is any lesion that presents as bright red velvety plaques, which cannot be characterized clinically or pathologically as any other recognizable condition (WHO). Most of these lesions are carcinoma in situ or frank carcinoma and are found at high-risk sites (at least 85%).

This lesion has been diagnosed at an early stage compared with most oral carcinomas. Treatment is likely to be surgery, followed by radiotherapy with or without chemotherapy. If treated in the early stages, a 5-year survival rate of 85% or better can be achieved. If survival reaches 10 years, the patient is likely to be considered cured. However, 10% of patients with oral carcinoma develop a second primary lesion in the mouth or upper aerodigestive tract.

Approximately 25% of these deposits are not detectable clinically and are termed 'occult metastases'. If left untreated, they would continue to grow, ultimately invading beyond the lymph node and spreading to distant sites.

problems.description: Multiple tiny yellowish spots visible on the inner cheek lining — an incidental finding, present for as long as the patient can remember.
problems.etiology: Fordyce spots are **ectopic sebaceous glands** in the oral mucosa — sebaceous glands that developed at a site normally devoid of them [1]. They are a developmental variant, not a pathological process. Their number and size increase with age [2].
problems.presentation:
An incidental finding — the patient may ask about them, or you spot them during a routine examination.

What you see:

- **Tiny yellowish or cream-coloured spots** on the buccal mucosa, and occasionally the lip mucosa [1].
- They **occasionally cluster** into plaques that can resemble a white patch — but on close inspection, individual glands are visible within the cluster [1].
- **Present from childhood** — a patient who develops a similar lesion in adulthood should be investigated, not reassured as Fordyce [1].
problems.results:
No investigations needed in a typical presentation. The diagnosis is clinical:

- Slightly yellow rather than white.
- Bilateral, symmetrical distribution on the buccal mucosa.
- Present since childhood.
- Individual glands visible within any cluster.

If any doubt: biopsy will confirm sebaceous glands in the submucosal tissue.
problems.definingCharacteristics: Fordyce spots are distinguished from leukoplakia by their **yellow tinge**, the **visibility of individual gland openings**, and their **bilateral, symmetrical, and long-standing** nature [1]. Unlike any other white or yellowish lesion, they have been present since the patient was a child. They do not affect the lateral tongue — a Fordyce-like cluster on the lateral tongue should prompt investigation [1]. The distinction from chronic hyperplastic candidosis: no red component, no roughness, and the characteristic yellow appearance.
problems.treatment: None. **Reassurance only** [1]. Fordyce spots are a normal anatomical variant with no pathological potential.
problems.prognosis: Entirely benign. No risk of malignant transformation. No treatment required at any point.

citations.quote: Leukoedema and patches of Fordyce spots (sebaceous glands) are normal mucosal variants that affect primarily the buccal mucosa. Fordyce spots are sebaceous glands. They occasionally form clusters that resemble plaques but have a slightly yellow appearance, and individual glands are usually visible within the lesion. Both are present from childhood, and neither affects the lateral tongue.
With age, an ↑ occurs in the number and size of Fordyce's spots (sebaceous glands), lingual varices, and foliate papillae.

problems.description: Progressive tightening of the cheeks in a patient from South Asia who chews betel quid; trismus is developing.
problems.etiology:
A chronic, progressive fibrotic disease of the oral connective tissue, found predominantly in patients of South Asian origin who chew betel quid [1]. The mechanism: areca nut alkaloids drive hyperplasia of fibroblasts and elevated copper levels, leading to cross-linking of collagen by upregulation of lysyl oxidase and thus increased fibrosis and DNA damage [2]. Tobacco added to areca nut and slaked lime increases the risk of developing SCC [2].

Approximately 10% of the world's population use betel quid [3]. The buccal sulcus bears the brunt because the quid lies there for prolonged periods — many users sleep with a quid in the mouth [3].
problems.presentation:
The patient reports difficulty opening the mouth, which has developed over years. Burning sensation in the cheeks on eating is an early complaint [4].

What you see:

- **Pale, blanched buccal mucosa** with loss of the normal moist pink colour [5].
- **Vertical fibrous bands** palpable (and sometimes visible) just below the buccal mucosa when the mouth is opened — these feel hard [5].
- **Restricted mouth opening**: normal interincisal opening in adults is approximately 35 mm; in submucous fibrosis, this may be severely reduced (e.g. 17 mm) [6].
- Dark red/brown betel quid staining on the teeth [5].
- Red and atrophic areas in the mucosa — indicating underlying dysplasia [5].
problems.results:
- **Maximum voluntary interincisal opening** provides a baseline and monitors progression [6].
- **Biopsy**: required to assess dysplasia. Histology shows atrophic epithelium, dense submucosal fibrosis replacing the connective tissue, and muscle atrophy in advanced cases [7].
- Approximately one-third of patients with submucous fibrosis have oral white patches; dysplasia is present in the mucosa of **up to 16%** [8].
- **Malignant transformation to SCC occurs in 5–8%** of cases [8].
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The clinical picture is distinctive when the habit history is known: a South Asian patient with a long betel quid chewing history + progressive trismus + pale buccal mucosa with palpable vertical bands. The combination is virtually pathognomonic [1].

Distinguishing from lichen planus: oral lichen planus produces reticular striae or erosions but not trismus, not blanching fibrosis, and not the typical history of betel quid use.

The key clinical concern is that **trismus makes examination, detection, and treatment of concurrent malignancy extremely difficult** [8] — patients with submucous fibrosis who develop SCC have a poor prognosis because the cancer is often diagnosed late.
problems.treatment:
No treatment regimen yields fully satisfactory results [9].

- **Cessation of betel quid** is the single most important intervention [9].
- **Mouth opening exercises**: if patients commit to these, they may be spared the worst effects of extreme trismus [9].
- Intralesional steroid injections and surgery with flap reconstruction in severe cases [2].
- **Referral to a specialist centre**: mandatory, given the high risk of malignancy. All abnormal mucosa must be biopsied [9].
- Manage any concurrent carcinoma or dysplasia with the same modalities as in other patients (surgery, chemotherapy, radiotherapy) as allowed by the degree of trismus [9].
problems.prognosis: Malignant transformation occurs in **5–8%** of cases [8]. Trismus is often progressive and responds poorly to treatment in advanced disease; in extreme cases, incisor extractions may be required to allow feeding [8]. The prognosis for any oral carcinoma arising in the context of submucous fibrosis is very poor, mostly because late diagnosis is the norm [8]. Best outcomes are in patients diagnosed early with localized disease, who cease the habit and maintain mouth opening exercises [9].

citations.quote: The presentation and features are characteristic of oral submucous fibrosis. Gradual limitation of mouth opening and restriction of tongue movements are seen in a betel quid user who shows typical mucosal blanching and fibrosis presenting as bands in the buccal mucosa.

This is a condition found particularly in those of South Asian origin. It is characterized by chronic and progressive scarring of oral connective tissue due to hyperplasia of fibroblasts induced by chewing betel nuts (without tobacco). The addition of tobacco to areca nut and slake lime appears to ↑ the risk of developing SCC. The mucosa is pale, with constraining fibrous bands, and fibrosis of the submucosa occurs, making the lips and cheeks immobile and resulting in trismus. Pathogenesis is unclear; ↑ levels of copper due to areca nut chewing leading to cross-linking of collagen by upregulation of lysyl oxidase and thus ↑ fibrosis and DNA damage.

The quid is only chewed intermittently and lies in the buccal sulcus for long periods. Many users keep a quid in their mouth all day, and some even sleep with a quid in the mouth. It has been estimated that 10% of the world's population use betel quid, and chewing is a major health problem in many countries, including western societies with significant immigrant populations from endemic areas.

He has noticed the reduction in mouth opening over a period of several years but has never sought advice. It has not been overly painful, although during the same period, he has felt an uncomfortable burning sensation in the buccal mucosa on eating.

The buccal and soft palate mucosae are paler than normal. When the mouth is opened fully, thin white hard bands run vertically just below the buccal mucosa. These are just visible in the figure and are much more readily felt as hard ridges. Some of the less pale areas are red and atrophic.

The normal interincisal opening in an adult is approximately 35 mm. Measurement will provide a baseline reading against which to judge treatment efficacy or trismus progression. This patient can achieve a maximal voluntary interincisal opening of 17 mm.
The fibrosis involving deep muscle is consistent with the diagnosis of oral submucous fibrosis, and the overlying epithelium shows mild dysplasia.

Oral submucous fibrosis is a potentially malignant disorder. Approximately one-third of patients with submucous fibrosis have oral white patches, and dysplasia is present in the mucosa of up to 16%. Malignant transformation to squamous cell carcinoma occurs in 5–8% of cases. Limited opening is a major handicap in the diagnosis and treatment of malignancy and premalignant lesions. It makes examination, detection and treatment extremely difficult, and the prognosis for oral carcinoma in a patient with submucous fibrosis is very poor, mostly as a result of late diagnosis.

No treatment regimen yields satisfactory results, and the aim is maintenance of oral health and prevention of complications. If patients are committed to mouth opening exercises, they may be spared the worst effects of extreme trismus. The aims are best achieved by helping the patient with cessation of the habit and by detecting malignancy or dysplasia as early as possible. All abnormal mucosa must be regarded with the utmost suspicion and a biopsy performed.

problems.description: A smooth, fleshy lump on the inner cheek — sessile or stalked — that appeared after years of denture use or cheek biting.
problems.etiology: An over-vigorous connective tissue response to low-grade, recurrent trauma [1]. The thing is, the stimulus is usually chronic and minor: a denture flange, a sharp cusp, or habitual cheek biting. The tissue doesn't repair normally — it overreacts, producing a benign fibrous mass rather than simply healing flat [1].
problems.presentation: A smooth lump on the buccal mucosa, the colour of normal mucosa. It may be sessile (broad-based) or pedunculated (stalked), and ranges from a small discrete lump to, in extreme cases, a lesion covering the entire palate [1]. Usually painless.
problems.results: Diagnosis is clinical. Histology after excision confirms the picture: dense collagenous fibrous tissue lined by keratinized stratified squamous epithelium [1]. No investigation is required before excision in a typical presentation.
problems.definingCharacteristics: What sets this apart from other cheek lumps is the combination of a clear trauma history (denture or biting), a smooth surface with normal mucosa colour, and the soft-to-firm rubbery consistency of organised fibrous tissue. A vascular lesion will blanch on pressure; a fibroepithelial polyp won't. A mucocele sits in the floor of the mouth or lip and is fluctuant.
problems.treatment: Excise with base [1]. Include the base in the specimen to reduce the risk of recurrence and to allow full histological assessment. Address the underlying trauma source: adjust the denture, smooth the sharp cusp.
problems.prognosis: Excellent. Benign with no malignant potential. Recurrence is uncommon if the base is fully excised and the provoking trauma eliminated.

citations.quote: This is an over-vigorous response to low-grade recurrent trauma. May be sessile or pedunculated and ranges from small lumps to lesions covering the entire palate. Excise with base. Histology shows dense collagenous fibrous tissue lined by keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.

problems.description: A soft cheek lump — or mucosal swelling with lip involvement — in a patient with known or suspected Crohn's disease or sarcoidosis.
problems.conditionName: Oral granulomata (Crohn's disease / orofacial granulomatosis / sarcoidosis)
problems.etiology: These lumps are characterised histologically by granulomata — collections of epithelioid macrophages [1]. Several systemic conditions can drive the same picture: Crohn's disease, its localised oral-only variant orofacial granulomatosis (OFG), sarcoidosis, or implanted foreign material such as amalgam [1]. The reason they cluster in this origin is that the cheek mucosa is a common site for the presenting swelling.
problems.presentation: Soft mucosal swelling, often affecting the lips and buccal mucosa, with or without other signs of systemic disease. The patient may have a known GI diagnosis, or the oral swelling may be the first presentation.
problems.results: Biopsy is the key investigation: histology showing non-caseating granulomata confirms the diagnosis. The source of the granulomata — Crohn's, sarcoidosis, foreign body, or OFG — is then established by clinical context, imaging, and systemic workup.
problems.definingCharacteristics: Granulomatous swelling of the cheek or lip is a small differential. OFG is the localised variant when no systemic disease is found. The biopsy result (granulomata) is what separates this from fibroepithelial polyp, mucocele, and lymphoma. If amalgam particles are visible on the biopsy, foreign-body granuloma becomes the diagnosis.
problems.treatment: Treat or manage the underlying condition. Refer for systemic workup to exclude Crohn's, sarcoidosis, and other granulomatous diseases before committing to a purely localised diagnosis [1].
problems.prognosis: Depends on the underlying cause. OFG confined to the mouth can be managed with dietary exclusion and local measures. Crohn's and sarcoidosis require systemic management.

citations.quote: Lumps characterized by the histological finding of granulomata may be caused by Crohn's disease or its localized variant orofacial granulomatosis, sarcoidosis, or implanted foreign bodies such as amalgam.

problems.description: A blue or purple area on the cheek lining that blanches on pressure — present since childhood or early life.
problems.etiology: Developmental lesions of blood vessels, not neoplastic growths [1]. The distinction from haemangioma matters: vascular malformations do not regress — they grow with the patient, expanding slowly over a lifetime [1]. They are characterised by the rate of blood flow within the lesion: low-flow (venous, lymphatic) versus high-flow (arterial).
problems.presentation: A blue, purple, or reddish area on the buccal mucosa. Blanches on pressure (diascopy) because the blood can be displaced — this is the key clinical test. Soft and compressible. No pain unless thrombosed.
problems.results: Diascopy (pressing a glass slide against the lesion): a vascular lesion blanches. An amalgam tattoo or melanotic macule does not. Imaging (MRI or interventional radiology assessment) characterises the lesion and its flow before any intervention.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The blanching on diascopy is pathognomonic for a vascular lesion and immediately excludes pigmented lesions. The long-standing history from early life, and the absence of spontaneous regression, separate malformations from haemangiomas of infancy (which involute). Unlike pyogenic granuloma, vascular malformations are not rapidly growing and are not related to trauma.
problems.treatment: Interventional radiology and surgery [1]. Refer to the appropriate specialist centre — do not attempt to excise without characterising the lesion first, as high-flow lesions carry a significant haemorrhage risk.
problems.prognosis: Benign but persistent. Low-flow venous malformations are amenable to sclerotherapy or surgery. High-flow lesions are more challenging and require specialist intervention.

citations.quote: These are developmental lesions of blood vessels which do not regress but grow with the patient. Characterized by rate of blood flow in lesion. Rx: interventional radiology and surgery.

problems.description: A flat, blue-black discoloured patch on the inner cheek — not tender, not growing — in a patient with a history of amalgam restorations.
problems.etiology: Amalgam particles implanted into the oral mucosa — either at the time of placing or removing a restoration, or from a broken filling [1]. Fine fragments migrate into the connective tissue and remain there permanently, producing a localised blue/black pigmentation. Road traffic accidents involving grit, or pencil graphite, can produce similar-looking lesions [1].
problems.presentation: A dense blue or black area of mucosal pigmentation, localised and flat [1]. Usually adjacent to a tooth that carries or once carried an amalgam restoration. The lesion may be palpable but often is not [1]. Asymptomatic.
problems.results: Radiograph: amalgam tattoos are radio-opaque [1]. This is diagnostic — finding radio-opaque particles at the site of a pigmented lesion confirms amalgam, not melanoma. If no radio-opacity is seen and the site is not characteristic, biopsy is needed to exclude melanocytic lesions. The source notes: 'if asymptomatic, diagnose and reassure' [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics: Radio-opacity on plain radiograph is the distinguishing feature from all other pigmented lesions. Oral melanotic macule, melanoma, and drug-induced pigmentation are all radiolucent. The amalgam tattoo also tends to become granular and fragmented over time [1]. A lesion that is radio-opaque, flat, at a site consistent with a previous restoration, and longstanding needs no further investigation in a typical presentation.
problems.treatment: None required if asymptomatic: diagnose and reassure [1]. If removal is planned — cosmetically or to confirm the diagnosis — cut out as a full-thickness wedge [1]. Do not attempt shave excision: the granular fragments are embedded in the submucosal tissue.
problems.prognosis: Entirely benign. No transformation potential. Patients can be permanently reassured once the diagnosis is confirmed.

citations.quote: Amalgam tattoo is the commonest, a localized dense blue/black area of mucosal pigmentation. May result from implantation at time of restoration or from broken filling. Radio-opaque. May be palpable but often not. Amalgam tends to become granular and fragmented and if removal is planned, cut out as full-thickness wedge. If asymptomatic, diagnose and reassure. 'Road rash' from grit after road traffic accident or graphite from pencils can cause similar lesions.

problems.description: Large, deep mouth ulcers lasting weeks and leaving scars, in a patient with a long history of recurrent aphthous disease.
problems.etiology: A severe variant of recurrent aphthous stomatitis, seen in 10% of RAS patients [1]. The mechanism is the same T-cell-mediated immunological reaction as minor RAS, but with a greater degree of tissue destruction. Major aphthae have a higher association with gastrointestinal and haematological disorders, and are also seen in AIDS [1].
problems.presentation: Fewer ulcers than in the minor type, but each is large — more than 10 mm diameter — and painful [1]. They last 5–10 weeks and most commonly affect keratinized mucosa, though any site in the mouth and oropharynx may be affected [1]. Scarring on healing is characteristic. There is seldom a cyclical pattern as there is in minor RAS [1].
problems.results: Diagnosis is clinical: the size (>10 mm), duration (weeks), and eventual scarring distinguish this from the minor type. Haematological screening to exclude underlying gastrointestinal or haematological disease is indicated, as for all RAS — but here the association is even stronger [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics: The thing that separates major from minor RAS: size above 10 mm, duration of 5–10 weeks rather than 1–2 weeks, and healing with scarring rather than without [1]. Minor RAS virtually never produces a scar. Affects keratinized mucosa — unlike minor RAS which favours non-keratinized surfaces. The association with AIDS should prompt HIV testing if no other explanation is found.
problems.treatment: As for minor aphthae, plus topical or systemic steroids [1]. Screen for and treat any underlying haematological or GI disorder. Consider systemic immunomodulation in severe or refractory cases.
problems.prognosis: Major RAS is more difficult to manage than the minor form. Scarring from repeated ulceration can restrict mouth opening over time. Identifying and treating the underlying cause — where one exists — reduces severity.

citations.quote: Seen in 10% of RAS patients. A more severe and more frequent variant with fewer, but larger ulcers >10mm which may last 5–10 weeks and most commonly affect keratinized mucosa. Associated with tissue destruction and scarring, and any site in the mouth and oropharynx may be affected. There is an even higher association between major aphthae and gastrointestinal and haematological disorders. They are also seen in AIDS. Seldom a cyclical pattern. problems.description: Recurrent oral ulcers in a young adult alongside genital ulcers, skin lesions, or eye inflammation — seemingly unrelated symptoms presenting together.
problems.etiology: A severe relapsing and remitting systemic vasculitis that characteristically affects venules [1]. All organs of the body can be involved. It is most prevalent in the Far East, along the Silk Route, and in the Middle East; in the UK, a prevalence of 0.064 in 10,000 has been reported from Yorkshire [1]. A disease of young adults, more common and more severe in males, and associated with HLA-B51 [2].
problems.presentation: Oral ulcers are the most consistent feature and may be the presenting complaint [1][2]. The diagnosis is clinical and based on recurrent oral ulcers plus two of: skin lesions, uveitis, genital ulcers, or blistering of skin when cannulated [2]. No single diagnostic test exists [2].
problems.results: Diagnosis is clinical only — no pathognomonic test [2]. HLA-B51 association supports the diagnosis. Leucocytosis and raised ESR are common findings [1]. Multisystem involvement warrants full systemic workup.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The oral ulcers alone are indistinguishable from major RAS. The reason to think Behçet's is the combination: oral ulcers plus extraoral findings (genital ulcers, uveitis, skin lesions) [2]. The geographic background is a useful prompt — the condition is far commoner along the Silk Route than in northern Europe [1]. Sex predilection varies by region: Mediterranean 8:1 male predominance, European practice closer to 1:1 [2].
problems.treatment: Refer for multidisciplinary care [2]. Azathioprine, ciclosporin, and thalidomide are used in specialist settings [2]. The GDP's role is recognition and prompt referral — this is not a condition to manage in primary care.
problems.prognosis: A relapsing and remitting course, with the risk of serious systemic complications including uveitis leading to blindness and vascular involvement [1][2]. Prognosis depends on the organ systems involved.

citations.quote: A severe relapsing and remitting systemic vasculitis, characteristically affecting venules. All organs of the body can be affected. It has a worldwide distribution but is most prevalent in the Far East, along the Silk Route, and in the Middle East. In the UK a prevalence of 0.064 in 10,000 has been reported from Yorkshire. It is a disease of young adults, more common and more severe in males. It is associated with HLA subtype.

Oral ulcers with two of skin lesions, uveitis, genital ulcers, or blistering of skin when cannulated. Clinical Δ only. No tests, associated with HLA-B51. It is, in fact, a multisystem disease of immunological origin—need to recognize and refer for multidisciplinary care. It has a different sex predilection depending on the geographical region studied. M:F—Mediterranean 8:1, Far East 2:1, Europe 1:1. Azathioprine, ciclosporin, and thalidomide.

problems.description: Firm blisters on the cheek lining in an elderly patient, less fragile than those seen in pemphigus, with possible association to internal malignancy.
problems.etiology: An autoimmune condition caused by IgG autoantibodies directed against the epithelial basement membrane [1]. Subepithelial bullae form — the split is below the epithelium rather than within it, which is why the blisters are firmer and less likely to break down than those in pemphigus vulgaris [1]. Affects the over-60s age group [1]. May represent an external marker of internal malignancy, or may be a drug-related immune response [1].
problems.presentation: Firm, tense blisters on the oral mucosa, less fragile than those of pemphigus. The oral mucosa is affected in only around 20% of patients — skin is the more common site [1]. When oral lesions are present, they tend to be tense bullae rather than rapidly rupturing erosions.
problems.results: Biopsy with direct immunofluorescence: IgG deposits at the basement membrane zone confirm the diagnosis. The subepithelial cleft on histology distinguishes this from pemphigus (intraepithelial split).
problems.definingCharacteristics: Bullous pemphigoid differs from pemphigus vulgaris in three ways: the patient is older, the blisters are subepithelial and therefore firmer and more intact, and oral involvement is far less common (20% vs 95%) [1]. The possible association with internal malignancy or drug reactions should trigger a systemic review [1].
problems.treatment: Refer to dermatology or oral medicine for systemic management. Systemic corticosteroids are the mainstay. Investigate for underlying malignancy and review medications for drug-related triggers [1].
problems.prognosis: Generally more favourable than pemphigus — the condition can remit with treatment. However the association with internal malignancy and the age group means the overall prognosis depends on any underlying cause [1].

citations.quote: This affects the >60yrs age group. Subepithelial bullae form which are firm and less likely to break down than those in pemphigus; it is due to autoantibodies (IgG) to the epithelial basement membrane. The oral mucosa is only affected in ~20% of patients. May be an external 'marker' of internal malignancy or a drug-related immune response.

problems.description: Mouth blisters breaking down into large erosions in a middle-aged man with a known skin blistering condition linked to gluten.
problems.etiology: A rare chronic condition of unknown aetiology, frequently associated with gluten sensitivity [1]. Autoantibodies against reticulin, gliadin, endomysium, and transglutaminase are found [1]. Both skin and mucous membranes are affected. The condition is commoner in middle-aged men [1].
problems.presentation: Oral lesions are seen in 70% of patients who have a skin lesion [1]. Bullae in the mouth break down to leave large erosions — the blisters rupture quickly, so intact bullae are rarely seen on the buccal mucosa [1]. The skin blisters are the more prominent clinical feature.
problems.results: Autoantibody testing (anti-reticulin, anti-gliadin, anti-endomysium, anti-transglutaminase) supports the diagnosis. Skin biopsy with immunofluorescence showing IgA deposits at the dermal papillae is the gold standard for the skin diagnosis.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The interesting bit here is the diagnostic and therapeutic overlap: dapsone can be used both diagnostically and therapeutically [1] — a good response to dapsone supports the diagnosis. The gluten sensitivity link means a gluten-free diet helps [1]. These features separate it from pemphigus and bullous pemphigoid, where dapsone and gluten restriction have no role.
problems.treatment: Dapsone — both diagnostic and therapeutic [1]. A gluten-free diet helps [1]. Refer to dermatology for systemic management.
problems.prognosis: Chronic but manageable. Dapsone controls symptoms; a gluten-free diet may allow dose reduction over time [1].

citations.quote: This is a rare chronic condition of unknown aetiology, but often associated with gluten sensitivity with autoantibodies against reticullin, gliadin, endomysium, and transglutaminase. Oral lesions are seen in 70% of patients with a skin lesion. Commoner in middle-aged men; it affects both skin and mucous membranes; bullae in the mouth break down to leave large erosions. Rx: dapsone may be used both diagnostically and therapeutically. A gluten-free diet helps.

problems.description: Non-specific oral ulceration — occasionally with bullae — identified on biopsy as a distinct immunobullous disease separate from dermatitis herpetiformis.
problems.etiology: A rare condition identified pathologically rather than clinically [1]. It may be a variant of dermatitis herpetiformis — the clinical presentation overlaps but the immunofluorescence pattern is different: linear IgA deposits at the basement membrane zone, rather than the granular IgA of dermatitis herpetiformis [1].
problems.presentation: Produces non-specific oral ulceration; rarely, bullae are present in the mouth [1]. The oral presentation alone does not distinguish this from other blistering diseases — the diagnosis is histopathological.
problems.results: Biopsy with direct immunofluorescence is required for diagnosis: linear IgA deposits along the basement membrane zone is the defining finding [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics: Linear IgA disease cannot be distinguished from dermatitis herpetiformis, bullous pemphigoid, or other immunobullous conditions on clinical grounds alone — biopsy with immunofluorescence is needed [1]. The 'linear' refers to the pattern of IgA deposition, which contrasts with the granular pattern of dermatitis herpetiformis.
problems.treatment: Systemic steroids or mycophenolate mofetil [1]. Refer to dermatology.
problems.prognosis: The source is limited on prognosis beyond the treatment options. Systemic immunosuppression is required long term in most cases.

citations.quote: This is rare and identified pathologically. May be variant of dermatitis herpetiformis. Produces non-specific oral ulceration and rarely bullae. Systemic steroids or mycophenolate mofetil for Rx.

problems.description: Rapidly rupturing oral blisters leaving widespread raw erosions in a patient with confirmed or suspected pemphigus — often the mouth is the first site involved.
problems.etiology: A chronic autoimmune skin disease with a potential to be rapidly fatal if untreated: 10% mortality [1]. Patients carry IgG autoantibodies against desmosomal components, specifically desmoglein-1 and desmoglein-3 [1]. These antibodies disrupt the desmosomal tonofilament complex, causing acantholysis — individual epidermal cells lose their attachments to each other, and the epithelium falls apart from within [1].
problems.presentation: Oral mucosa is affected in 95% of patients with pemphigus vulgaris [1]. Critically, in 50% of patients, the mouth is the initial presentation — before skin lesions appear [1]. The blisters are intraepithelial and fragile: they rupture almost immediately on formation, leaving raw, painful erosions. What you see in practice are erosions rather than intact bullae.
problems.results: Biopsy with immunofluorescence: intraepithelial IgG deposits and acantholysis on histology confirm the diagnosis. Circulating autoantibodies to epithelial desmosome tonofilament are detectable in serum [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics: The reason pemphigus is so dangerous is that the 10% mortality reflects the severity of the disease before systemic immunosuppression [1]. The oral lesions presenting first in 50% means the GDP may be the first clinician to see the condition — biopsy and urgent referral are mandatory [1]. Distinguishing from bullous pemphigoid: the blisters in pemphigus are intraepithelial and rupture immediately; in bullous pemphigoid they are subepithelial and much firmer.
problems.treatment: Refer urgently to dermatology. Systemic immunosuppression is required — high-dose corticosteroids and steroid-sparing agents. The mortality risk means delay is unacceptable [1].
problems.prognosis: Mortality 10% without treatment [1]. With modern systemic immunosuppression, the condition can be controlled, though patients typically require long-term therapy. Oral mucosal healing tracks systemic disease control.

citations.quote: Pemphigus is a chronic skin disease which can be rapidly fatal if not treated (mortality 10%). Affected patients have immunoglobulin G (IgG) autoantibodies against desmosomal components like desmoglein-1 and desmoglein-3. Oral mucosa is affected in 95% of patients with pemphigus vulgaris (most common type) and may be the initial presentation of pemphigus in 50%. problems.description: Blistering and large raw erosions on the cheek mucosa in a patient with a known lichen planus diagnosis — bullae forming unexpectedly.
problems.etiology: A rare variant of oral lichen planus in which subepithelial bullae form and then break down, leaving large erosions [1]. It affects both skin and mucous membranes [1]. The background autoimmune T-cell attack on stratified squamous epithelia is shared with all forms of lichen planus.
problems.presentation: Bullae form on the buccal mucosa (and potentially elsewhere) and rupture to leave raw, painful erosions [1]. Intact blisters may be seen briefly, but the predominant picture is one of erosion and ulceration on a background of lichen planus changes.
problems.results: Biopsy: subepithelial bullae are the defining histological finding, in the context of the dense lymphocytic band and basal cell degeneration typical of lichen planus. This distinguishes it from pemphigus (intraepithelial) and bullous pemphigoid (subepithelial but with IgG basement-membrane antibodies).
problems.definingCharacteristics: Bullous lichen planus is a rare variant, but it sits within a lichen planus context — look for the reticular striae elsewhere in the mouth [1]. The blistering is what surprises: typical reticular lichen planus doesn't blister. This variant behaves more like the erosive type in clinical severity. The background lichen planus changes in the same patient are the diagnostic anchor.
problems.treatment: Treat as for erosive lichen planus: topical and systemic corticosteroids, and referral to oral medicine or dermatology for 6-monthly surveillance [1].
problems.prognosis: The source notes the erosive variant of lichen planus carries a small premalignant risk (<1%) [1]. This warrants the same 6-monthly follow-up as the erosive type.

citations.quote: This affects both skin and mucous membranes. Bullous lichen planus is a rare variant in which subepithelial bullae form and break down, leaving large erosions.

problems.description: A red, ulcerated, or glazed area on the cheek mucosa in a patient with lichen planus — painful and slow to respond to topical treatment.
problems.etiology: A comparatively rare variant of lichen planus [1]. The background autoimmune process is shared with all lichen planus types — T-cell attack on stratified squamous epithelium — but the erosive variant produces mucosal breakdown rather than the hyperkeratotic striae of the reticular type.
problems.presentation: Erythematous, glazed, or ulcerated areas on the buccal mucosa, often painful. The reticular striae typical of the commoner lichen planus may be visible at the periphery of the erosive zones. The patient usually reports a burning discomfort aggravated by food, particularly acidic or spicy items.
problems.results: Biopsy when the diagnosis is uncertain or when dysplasia needs to be excluded. Some authorities classify erosive lichen planus as premalignant — the source acknowledges a risk of less than 1% [1]. Malignant surveillance is indicated.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The reason this entry exists separately from reticular lichen planus is the premalignant designation: the common reticular form carries no proven premalignant potential, but the erosive variant does [1]. A patient who presents with erosive rather than reticular changes needs a different management pathway — 6-monthly follow-up rather than reassurance alone. The common forms of lichen planus have no proven premalignant potential; this is the exception [1].
problems.treatment: Topical corticosteroids as first line (betamethasone mouthwash or dexamethasone). Oral medicine or dermatology referral and 6-monthly follow-up to exclude malignant transformation [1].
problems.prognosis: Some authorities classify erosive lichen planus as premalignant with a transformation risk of less than 1% [1]. Regular surveillance is warranted. Symptomatic control with topical steroids is achievable for most patients.

citations.quote: This is a comparatively rare variant of lichen planus, which some authorities believe to be premalignant (<1%). The common forms of lichen planus have no proven premalignant potential.

problems.description: A lichen-planus-like white or ulcerated patch on the cheek that appeared after starting a new medication — often gold, NSAIDs, or beta blockers.
problems.etiology: A drug-induced immunological reaction producing oral lesions that are clinically and histologically identical to lichen planus [1]. The classic association is gold (used in rheumatoid arthritis), but NSAIDs, oral hypoglycaemics, and beta blockers are commoner offenders in practice [1].
problems.presentation: White, striated, or erosive lesions on the buccal mucosa — identical in appearance to lichen planus. The distribution may be asymmetric, acute in onset, or more extensively ulcerated than typical lichen planus. A careful drug history is the key diagnostic step.
problems.results: Medication review: identify the offending drug and correlate its introduction or dose change with the onset of the lesion [1]. Biopsy may be needed to exclude dysplasia. Resolution or improvement after withdrawing the suspected drug supports the diagnosis.
problems.definingCharacteristics: What separates a drug lichenoid reaction from true lichen planus is the history: acute onset following drug initiation, asymmetric distribution, and possible resolution on drug withdrawal [1]. The classic bilateral symmetry and posterior buccal distribution of true lichen planus may be absent. Identifying and removing the drug is both diagnostic and therapeutic.
problems.treatment: Identify and withdraw the offending drug if possible [1]. Consult with the prescribing physician before stopping any medication. Topical steroids for symptomatic relief while the drug is being rationalised.
problems.prognosis: Good if the offending drug is identified and stopped — lesions typically improve or resolve. If the drug cannot be withdrawn, manage symptomatically as for erosive lichen planus.

citations.quote: Classically associated with the use of gold in the Rx of rheumatoid arthritis. NSAIDs, oral hypoglycaemics, and beta blockers are commoner offenders.

problems.description: Severe, painful oral ulceration developing in a patient on long-term medication — chloramphenicol, certain analgesics, or phenytoin — with no healing in sight.
problems.etiology: A range of drugs can depress cell lines in the haemopoietic system, and the effects reach the oral mucosa [1]. Phenytoin, for example, used long-term, depletes folate leading to macrocytic anaemia, which in turn produces severe aphthous stomatitis [1]. Chloramphenicol and certain analgesics can induce agranulocytosis — the loss of neutrophils removes normal mucosal defences and severe oral ulceration follows [1].
problems.presentation: Severe, slow-healing ulceration that does not fit the typical minor RAS pattern in a patient on a relevant medication. The ulcers may be very large, very painful, and completely unresponsive to standard topical treatments.
problems.results: Full blood count is essential: agranulocytosis will show as a profound neutropaenia; macrocytic anaemia from folate deficiency will be apparent on the blood film [1]. Drug history cross-referenced with the BNF is key to identifying the culprit.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The reason to think drug-induced ulceration rather than major RAS is the medication context: a patient on phenytoin, chloramphenicol, or analgesics with a history of worsening ulceration that appeared or intensified after starting the drug [1]. The FBC result clinches it — a normal white cell count and film make drug-induced marrow suppression unlikely. Cross-referencing the drug history with the BNF is the practical first step [1].
problems.treatment: Identify and review the offending medication with the prescribing physician [1]. For agranulocytosis: urgent medical referral for haematological assessment and management. Treat folate deficiency if confirmed.
problems.prognosis: Depends on the degree of marrow suppression and whether the drug can be stopped. Chloramphenicol can also induce aplastic anaemia, which affects haemostasis and can cause spontaneous oral purpura — a more severe and harder-to-reverse outcome [1].
